Case Study 2-1

Progressive distal weakness & atrophy in a 17-year-old — worked word-for-word from the case document, with small-group discussion and clinical reasoning threaded in as annotations.

👤 17 y/o male ⏱️ Insidious · 3 yr course 📍 Bilateral, distal > proximal 🧬 Family Hx positive 🎯 Working dx: CMT1A
Annotation key Localization Exam finding Terminology Pattern recognition Genetics / workup Hover a highlight for a quick peek · tap for the full note
Chief Complaint HCC Family Hx ROS Gen. PE Neuro Exam Follow-up Clinical Reasoning Concept Deep-Dives

Chief Complaint

This is a 17-year-old male high school student presenting with progressively worsening weakness and muscle atrophy in the lower extremities.

History of Chief Complaint

He is the product of a normal pregnancy and an uneventful delivery. He achieved his developmental milestones on time. His mother notes that he always seemed clumsy and did not do well in sports activity although he loves sports and tries very hard. He has suffered three sprained ankles while playing soccer. His legs always appeared very thin and recently the high school physical education instructor became concerned and asked for a physician's evaluation.

The patient notes that over the past three years he thinks he has experienced a gradual increase in weakness in his lower extremities and states that he now finds it difficult to run the length of the soccer field. He complains that even walking can be difficult on occasion and that he frequently trips especially at night or in dimly lit areas. His mother notes that over the past year he has developed a very loud sounding gait.

Family History

The patient's mother and father are alive and in good health. He has a 10-year-old brother who also has reduced muscle mass in his legs. His mother's uncle has very thin legs and complains of feeling tired and weak when having to walk any distance.

Medical History

Positive for a tonsillectomy at 10 years of age; all vaccinations are up to date.

Allergies

NKA

Review of Systems

GENERAL: Patient denies any recent weight change but admits to progressive loss of strength in his legs. SKIN: He denies any rashes or sores on his skin. HEENT: denies headache, head injury, or dizziness. Denies changes in vision or eye pain. He denies changes in hearing, tinnitus or ear pain. He admits to an occasional cold with runny nose but denies nosebleeds, sore throat or dental pain. NECK: denies swelling or stiffness. RESPIRATORY: Denies cough or dyspnea. CARDIOVASCULAR: Denies chest pain or palpitations. ABDOMINAL: Denies dysphagia or odynophagia, admits to normal colored stools once a day. Denies any abdominal pain. URINARY: Denies any hematurea, frequency or urgency. Denies any flank pain. GENITAL: Denies discharge or pain. Admits to sexual activity, denies any rashes or sores. MUSCULOSKELETAL: admits to muscle cramping and muscle pain in the lower extremity especially the calves, admits to pain in the arch of both feet while walking. NEUROLOGIC: Denies any changes in mood or any depression. Denies blackouts and dizziness, denies any loss of sensation or strength in the upper extremity. Admits to loss of strength in the lower extremity and a blunting of feeling in his legs but mainly in his feet. Admits to feeling unsteady when walking and to frequently tripping on small objects especially at night.

General Physical Examination

The patient is awake, oriented and cooperative with pleasant affect. His blood pressure is 121/79, heart rate is 61, respirations are 16 and temperature is 98.6°F. HEAD & NECK: Head is normocephalic, pupils are equal and reactive to light. Auditory canals are patent and non-reddened. Nose, mouth and pharynx are clear without tenderness. Neck has normal range of motion and without lymphadenopathy. CARDIOVASCULAR: regular rate and rhythm, normal apex beat, no jugular-venous distention. There is an audible carotid pulse with no bruits. ABDOMINAL: mild abdominal obesity with no masses or tenderness palpable. MUSCULOSKELETAL: Extremities are four in number without tenderness except in the feet. No pretibial edema. No joint swelling. Notable atrophy is present in the calf region of the lower extremity bilaterally. His arches are markedly elevated and his toes are blunt and square in shape. SKIN: No rashes, ecchymosis, petechiae.

Neurologic Examination

Mental Status. Patient is awake and oriented to person, place and time. His mood is appropriate and memory and speech are intact.

Cranial Nerves. Cranial nerves 1–12 were intact.

Motor Systems. Strength and reflexes were intact everywhere in the upper extremities. Muscle bulk was intact in the upper extremities. Strength was 4/5 for flexion and extension at the hip and knee bilaterally and 3/5 for dorsi- and plantar flexion at the right ankle and 2/5 for dorsi- and plantar flexion at the left ankle. Deep tendon reflexes were 1/4 at the knee and trace at the ankle bilaterally. Gait was slightly wide-based with occasional audible foot slapping. Heel-to-shin testing was normal with eyes open but abnormal with eyes closed.

Sensory Exam. Sensory was intact in the upper extremities. In the lower extremities, vibration sense and position sense were diminished about the knee and absent about the ankle and foot. Two-point discrimination was absent on the sole of the foot but present about the ankle and knee. Response to pinprick was intact throughout the upper and lower extremities.

Follow-up Examination

Six months later the weakness in the lower extremity worsened slightly, with strength being 2/5 for dorsi- and plantar flexion bilaterally. Diminution of 2-point discrimination was now observable about the knee bilaterally. He is beginning to complain of a perceived weakness in his hands.

Clinical Reasoning Walkthrough

Condensed from the small-group discussion + the OpenEvidence breakdown of the 11 standard localization questions. Read top to bottom: where it is → what it is → how you'd prove it → what happens next.

01 · Localization

Segmental, not suprasegmental

Intact mentation, cranial nerves, and vision rule out cortex, brainstem, and cranial nerve disease. Hyporeflexia + atrophy + flaccid weakness (no spasticity, no Babinski) rule out an upper motor neuron / corticospinal lesion. Everything points to the peripheral nervous system — nerve roots, plexus, or peripheral nerve.

02 · Distribution

Diffuse, length-dependent, symmetric

Bilateral, distal > proximal, worst in the longest nerves (feet) and not yet reaching the (shorter) nerves to the hands. Not focal (one lesion), not multifocal (scattered lesions) — this is the textbook signature of a symmetric polyneuropathy.

03 · Time course

Insidious, chronically progressive

No identifiable onset day — mom anchors it to school sports performance over years, not an event. Measured in months–years, not hours (stroke) or days–weeks (GBS/CIDP). Confirmed objectively by the 6-month follow-up showing further decline.

04 · Differential diagnosis

Ranking the possibilities

DiagnosisFitsArgues against
CMT1A most likely Adolescent onset, distal>proximal weakness+atrophy, pes cavus, large-fiber sensory loss, hyporeflexia, AD-pattern family Hx —
CMT2 (axonal) Clinically near-identical to CMT1 NCS distinguishes: CMT2 has near-normal velocity, low amplitude
Distal HMN Distal weakness/atrophy pattern Pure motor — this patient has clear sensory loss
Friedreich ataxia Pes cavus, sensory ataxia, areflexia No dysarthria, cerebellar signs, extensor plantars, cardiomyopathy, or scoliosis; AR not AD pedigree
CIDP (acquired) Can mimic distal weakness clinically Subacute (wks–mo) not lifelong; this patient's course + family Hx favor hereditary
Cord compression — No UMN signs, no sensory level, no bowel/bladder involvement
B12 deficiency Can hit posterior columns Usually mixed UMN+LMN; unusual in a healthy 17-year-old
05 · Diagnostic workup

How you'd actually prove it

1
NCS / EMG first. This is the branch point.
Motor NCV <38 m/s, uniform slowing → demyelinating (CMT1)  |  NCV >38 m/s, reduced amplitude → axonal (CMT2)
2
Genetic testing, guided by NCS.
Demyelinating → PMP22 duplication first (>50% of CMT1) → if neg: GJB1, MPZ  |  Axonal → MFN2 (CMT2A)  |  Still negative → NGS panel (100+ genes)
3
Labs to exclude acquired mimics.
Fasting glucose/HbA1c, B12 + metabolites, SPEP/immunofixation, CBC, TSH
4
Family evaluation.
NCS on the affected brother ± maternal uncle supports the hereditary diagnosis and clarifies inheritance
06 · Prognosis

Slow, but not benign to ignore

Decades-long progression; >95% remain ambulatory; normal lifespan. Weakness/atrophy spread proximally and reach the hands; foot deformity worsens; decline may accelerate after age 50. No disease-modifying therapy yet — management is entirely supportive.

07 · Management

Multidisciplinary, symptomatic

  • AFOs for foot drop + gait stability
  • Supportive footwear / custom orthotics
  • PT: stretching + moderate strengthening (avoid high-resistance)
  • OT as hand involvement progresses
  • Ortho referral for severe pes cavus
  • Neuropathic pain: gabapentin / pregabalin / TCA
  • Genetic counseling for patient + family
  • Fall prevention — this patient's real vulnerability is the dark

Concept Deep-Dives

The underlying neuroanatomy this case is built on — pulled from small-group, worth knowing cold.

Coordination

The cerebellum's three inputs

Lose proprioception (this patient) and vision quietly takes over the job. Kill the lights and the backup system is gone too — that's why he trips at night. A true cerebellar lesion would look ataxic with eyes open or closed.

Distribution

Length-dependent "dying back"

Longest axons fail first because they have the most membrane to maintain. Feet go first (already severe at presentation); hands are next in line — and right on cue, this patient starts noticing hand weakness at the 6-month follow-up.

Peripheral fibers

Which fiber, which finding

FiberDiameter / myelinSpeedCarriesIn this case
Aα Largest, thickly myelinated Fastest Motor to skeletal muscle; muscle spindle & GTO (reflex arcs) Reflexes lost early — knee 1/4, ankle trace
Aβ Large, myelinated Fast Vibration, position sense, 2-point discrimination (dorsal columns) Lost distally first — the core sensory finding here
Aδ Small, thinly myelinated Medium Fast/sharp pain Pinprick intact — small fibers spared
C Smallest, unmyelinated (shared Schwann cell) Slowest Slow/dull pain, temperature Not tested, but pattern predicts sparing
Reference · fiber classification
Reference · motor / sensory / autonomic

This large-fiber-predominant, small-fiber-sparing pattern is the sensory fingerprint of CMT — the opposite of what you'd see in a small-fiber neuropathy like early diabetic neuropathy.

Sign-sorting

UMN vs. LMN — this case is all LMN

UMNLMN ✓ this pt
Tone↑ spastic↓ flaccid
Reflexes↑ hyperreflexia, clonus↓ hyporeflexia
BabinskiPresentAbsent
AtrophyMinimal, lateProminent, early
FasciculationsNoYes

Not one UMN feature appears anywhere in this case. That absence is doing as much diagnostic work as the positive findings.

Genetics

Autosomal dominant, PMP22 duplication

Two generations back on the maternal line, a great-uncle is affected. The mother herself shows no signs of disease, yet both her children do — the classic look of a non-penetrant carrier: she inherited the PMP22 duplication but never expressed it, and passed it on regardless. That's how an autosomal dominant pedigree can appear to "skip" a generation without actually breaking AD inheritance.

The mutation itself — a PMP22 gene duplication on chromosome 17 — is the single most common cause of hereditary neuropathy, accounting for >50% of all CMT.

Electrodiagnostics

Reading the NCS: demyelinating vs. axonal

CMT1 (demyelinating)
NCV < 38 m/s, uniform slowing
CMT2 (axonal)
NCV near-normal, ↓ amplitude

Uniform slowing across nerves points to a hereditary process. Patchy slowing, conduction block, or temporal dispersion instead points toward an acquired demyelinating process like CIDP — a key discriminator when the clinical picture alone is ambiguous.

Histology · CMT1A

Onion bulbs — the histology signature of CMT1A

Hypertrophic neuropathy in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A — sural nerve biopsy from a 39-year-old woman (Thionin and acridine orange, bar = 20 μm). There is extensive "onion bulb" formation due to Schwann cell multiplication. The axons within the onion bulbs vary from being demyelinated (arrow) through thin myelin to thickly myelinated fibres. There are occasional regenerative clusters (asterisk). Endoneurial collagen is increased.

Onion bulbs form from repeated cycles of demyelination and Schwann cell–driven remyelination — the cellular response to the PMP22 duplication in CMT1A. Layer after layer of Schwann cell processes wrap each axon concentrically, thickening the nerve (this is the "hypertrophic" in hypertrophic neuropathy) and producing the uniform conduction slowing seen on NCS. This is the structural reason CMT1's electrodiagnostic signature (uniform NCV <38 m/s) looks so different from an axonal process like CMT2.

Nerve anatomy

Fascicle architecture, on biopsy

The connective-tissue layers a sural nerve biopsy actually cuts through: epineurium wraps the whole nerve, perineurium wraps each fascicle, and endoneurium surrounds individual axon–Schwann cell units within it. Onion bulbs (previous card) form inside this endoneurial space.

Ultrastructure

Unmyelinated (C) fibers, under EM

Small unmyelinated axons (Ax) bundle together inside pockets of a single Schwann cell — a Remak bundle — rather than each getting its own myelin wrap. This is the structural reason C fibers conduct slowly regardless of disease state, and part of why small-fiber function (temperature, dull/slow pain) is the last thing lost in a large-fiber-predominant process like this patient's.

Spinal nerve anatomy

Roots, rami, and ganglia

Dorsal / ventral roots & rami
Somatic / visceral afferent & efferent

The dorsal root carries sensory afferents into the cord, with cell bodies sitting just outside it in the dorsal root ganglion (this is where the vibration/position/2-point-discrimination signal in this case is already in trouble before it even reaches the cord). The ventral root carries motor efferents out. Both merge into the spinal nerve, then redistribute through the dorsal and ventral rami to skin, muscle, and joints — the anatomic basis for testing a specific root/level on NCS.

Pain pathway

Where pinprick actually goes: Aδ vs. C fiber

Dorsal horn laminae & Lissauer's tract
Spinothalamic projection

Both pain fiber types enter through the dorsal root ganglion and synapse in the dorsal horn (substantia gelatinosa, laminae I–II) before crossing and ascending as the spinothalamic tract. Aδ fibers are thinly myelinated and fast — first, sharp, well-localized pain. C fibers are unmyelinated and slow — the dull, aching pain that follows. Pinprick in this case tests the Aδ pathway, and it's intact — consistent with this being a large-fiber-selective process rather than something hitting pain fibers too.

Clinical gestalt

What it actually looks like on exam

Lower limb
Upper limb (later disease)

Everything in the lower-limb panel is already in this case (pes cavus, hammer/claw toes, calf atrophy). The upper-limb panel — hand wasting, claw-hand deformity — is where this patient is headed, not where he is yet: at follow-up he's only just starting to notice hand weakness. That's the stocking→glove progression arriving in real time.
